stem: A scientist creates a knockout mouse lacking platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM-1), which is normally expressed at endothelial cell junctions.  Which of the following steps in neutrophil extravasation is most likely impaired in this mouse model?​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​
explanation:
Inflammation is an important process in the defense against various pathogens.  It is characterized by the passage of leukocytes into the inflamed tissue (ie, extravasation).  The following steps are involved in inflammatory leukocyte accumulation:

  1. Margination:  Increased vascular leakage in the microvasculature leads to hemoconcentration and decreased wall shear stress, improving the contact of neutrophils with the endothelial lining.

  2. Rolling:  Neutrophils roll on the endothelium via low-affinity binding between selectins and the carbohydrate ligand sialyl Lewis X (sLeX).  E-selectin and P-selectin on endothelial cells bind sLeX displayed on neutrophil glycoproteins (eg, PSGL-1), while L-selectin on neutrophils binds sLeX-bearing ligands on the endothelium.  Cytokine stimulation (eg, TNF-α, IL-1) greatly increases expression of endothelial selectins.

  3. Activation:  Slow rolling allows the leukocytes to sample the chemokines secreted by the inflamed tissue.  This activates integrins by inducing a signaling cascade that results in a conformational change in the integrins necessary for binding.

  4. Tight adhesion and crawling:  Neutrophils become firmly attached to the endothelium via the binding of CD18-containing beta-2 integrins (eg, Mac-1, LFA-1) to intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) on endothelial cells.  This allows the firmly adherent neutrophil to crawl along the endothelial surface to an intercellular junction.

  5. Transmigration:  After crawling to the endothelial cell periphery, neutrophils migrate out of the vasculature (diapedesis) by squeezing in between the cells via integrin attachments and adherence to platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM-1).  This protein is found primarily at the peripheral intercellular junctions of endothelial cells.

Defects in this cascade cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD), a group of rare autosomal recessive disorders in which leukocytes cannot leave the vasculature to reach inflamed tissue.  The most common form, LAD type 1, results from absent CD18 and therefore an inability to synthesize the beta-2 integrins Mac-1 and LFA-1, impairing tight adhesion, crawling, and transmigration.  Manifestations include recurrent skin infections with no pus formation, delayed umbilical cord detachment, and poor wound healing.

Educational objective:Inflammation is characterized by the passage of circulating inflammatory leukocytes into the inflamed tissue.  The steps involved include margination, rolling, activation, tight adhesion and crawling, and transmigration.  Transmigration (diapedesis) between endothelial cells requires PECAM-1, located at endothelial intercellular junctions.​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​
